sources_considered.why: Contemporaneous peer-reviewed watermarking research challenges an absolute denial of automated identification, but has bounded coverage.
Contemporaneous technical review distinguishes provenance tracking, automated detection, and human-assisted detection.
Prepublication benchmark directly compares human and machine image detection and documents sensitivity to downsampling.
Confirms that the benchmark was publicly submitted on December 12, 2024.
Current documentation includes later capabilities and cannot establish the December 2024 state.
Current, unversioned documentation was not used to infer historical capability.

evidence_items.explanation: A functioning automated identification method existed before publication, challenging a literal human-only assertion. Identifying text bearing this watermark does not establish provenance for arbitrary unmarked content or allow users to avoid all AI content.

evidence_items.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology

receipt.public_excerpt: only perform well on specific generators.

evidence_items.explanation: NIST documents limits on general detection and reviews human results ranging from strong performance in some settings to chance-level performance in others. This supports caution but establishes neither universal unavoidability nor a generally reliable human exception.

The benchmark found that machine performance depended strongly on image processing and that humans outperformed the tested detector on the study images. It did not test unrestricted provenance investigation or whether ordinary users could avoid AI content.

unresolved_gaps: No representative study establishing unavoidable exposure during ordinary online activity was found.
No evaluation establishes reliable considered human scrutiny across arbitrary images and text.
Bounded watermark detection does not settle the broader claim about arbitrary content provenance.
